questions.prompt: Compass and straightedge only; leave all arcs. Construct an angle with vertex P and one side ray PR that is congruent to ∠ABC.

questions.standard_level: Geometry. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Geometry, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Compass and straightedge only; leave all arcs. Construct an angle at P on ray PR whose measure is twice m∠ABC.
questions.prompt_markup:
Compass and straightedge only; leave all arcs.
Construct an angle at P on ray PR whose measure is twice m∠ABC.
questions.correct_answer: Copy ∠ABC onto ray PR to get ray PG, then copy ∠ABC again onto ray PG (on the other side from R) to get ray PH; ∠RPH = 2∠ABC.
questions.grading_note: Grade the construction marks, not only the final figure: two complete angle copies sharing ray PG.

questions.skill: Justify why the angle-copy construction works
questions.standard_level: Geometry. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Geometry, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.response: write the answer and show the required work
questions.prompt: In copying ∠ABC to ∠FPG, BD = BE = PF = PG (same arc radius) and DE = FG (same compass setting). Prove that ∠DBE ≅ ∠FPG.
questions.prompt_markup: In copying ∠ABC to ∠FPG, BD = BE = PF = PG (same arc radius) and DE = FG (same compass setting). Prove that ∠DBE ≅ ∠FPG.
questions.required_method: Prove △DBE ≅ △FPG by SSS, then use corresponding angles.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: BD = PF, BE = PG, DE = FG (construction); SSS; corresponding angles ∠DBE and ∠FPG.

questions.prompt: ∠XYZ is copied to vertex Q, opening downward: an arc of radius r centered at Y meets the sides at U and V, the same arc centered at Q meets the given ray at U′, and an arc of radius UV centered at U′ meets it at V′. Prove that ∠U′QV′ ≅ ∠XYZ.

questions.prompt: In copying ∠ABC to P, a student keeps the arc radius but sets the compass to BD (a radius) instead of the chord DE for the last arc. Which step of the SSS justification fails, and what goes wrong with the copy?
questions.prompt_markup: In copying ∠ABC to P, a student keeps the arc radius but sets the compass to BD (a radius) instead of the chord DE for the last arc. Which step of the SSS justification fails, and what goes wrong with the copy?
questions.correct_answer: The third pair of sides is no longer DE = FG, so SSS does not apply; the new ray makes a 60° angle (an equilateral triangle) instead of ∠ABC unless ∠ABC is 60°.

questions.standard_level: Geometry. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Geometry, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.response: write the answer and show the required work
questions.prompt: Explain why the angle-copy construction works using a rigid motion instead of SSS: there is a rigid motion taking B to P and ray BC onto ray PR.
questions.prompt_markup: Explain why the angle-copy construction works using a rigid motion instead of SSS: there is a rigid motion taking B to P and ray BC onto ray PR.
questions.correct_answer: The motion sends E to F (same radius on ray PR) and D to the point on the arc at P that is DE from F on the chosen side, which is G; so ∠ABC → ∠FPG.
questions.required_method: Follow D, E, F, G under the rigid motion and use the fact that two circles meet in at most one point on each side of a line.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: rigid motions keep the distances BD, BE, DE; the image of D is on the arc at P and DE from F; on one side of line PR that point is G.

questions.prompt: Compass and straightedge only; leave all arcs. Construct the line through P parallel to line ℓ by copying an angle.
questions.prompt_markup:
